content.title: About
content.content: Salami is a cured sausage made from pork and/or beef, seasoned with spices and aged for several weeks to months. The hard, sliced version has a rich aroma, firm texture, and a slightly spicy flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Salami originated in Italy in the 19th century and quickly spread across Europe and the United States.
Traditional recipes use a blend of pork and beef together with red wine.
Hard salami is aged longer than soft varieties, giving it a more intense taste.
Sliced pieces are convenient for sandwiches, appetizers, and antipasto platters.
There are over 30 regional varieties of salami, each with its own spice blend.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Salami provides high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron in salami helps maintain normal hemoglobin levels and energy.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: B12 and B6 vitamins support nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Zinc content
items.content: Zinc contributes to immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Probiotic bacteria
items.content: Fermentation during production can promote beneficial microbes.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Salami is typically high in salt, which can raise blood pressure if consumed in excess.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Hard salami is rich in saturated fats, which should be limited in heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Nitrites and nitrates
items.content: These preservatives are used to maintain color and prevent bacterial growth but may be harmful in large amounts.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to meat proteins.

items.title: Shelf‑life control
items.content: Improper storage can lead to growth of pathogens such as Salmonella or Listeria.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Thinly sliced salami is perfect for sandwiches, salads, pasta, pizza, or as part of a cold‑cut platter. It can also be lightly pan‑fried to enhance its flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep salami in its original packaging or an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0 °C–4 °C. For longer storage, it can be frozen, but it is best used within 1–2 months. Prevent exposure to air to avoid drying out.
